name: Risk Identification
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Naming the Landmine Before Someone Steps on It: Risk Identification
lesson.summary: Risk identification is the ATAM activity of flagging specific architectural decisions that could lead to future problems, turning a general sense of unease into a documented, traceable statement the team can act on.
lesson.body:
An architecture risk, as the earlier chapter established, is a decision made during design that has the potential to cause problems later, whether or not it has caused any problem yet. Risk identification is the concrete activity of finding and writing down those decisions during an ATAM evaluation. It happens as the review team walks the highest priority quality attribute scenarios from the utility tree through the actual architecture, checking at each sensitivity and tradeoff point whether the decision made there looks sound or looks like it is quietly setting up a future failure.

A well formed risk statement names the specific decision, the quality attribute scenario it threatens, and the reasoning connecting the two. Consider a decentralized lending protocol whose smart contracts pull an asset's current price from a single exchange's on chain liquidity pool. Risk identification would flag this as a risk against the security quality attribute scenario covering manipulation: an attacker who can temporarily distort the price on that one pool, for instance by borrowing a large amount of an asset for a single transaction, can trick the lending contract into mispricing collateral and draining funds. This is not hypothetical; DeFi protocols relying on a single, easily moved price source have been exploited this way in real, documented incidents, including the bZx protocol attacks that manipulated thinly traded markets to distort the price feeds contracts relied on.

Risk identification is deliberately not the same activity as fixing the risk. An ATAM evaluation records the risk, its severity, and which scenario it threatens, but resolving it is a separate step covered later as risk mitigation. Keeping identification and mitigation separate matters because it stops a review from quietly narrowing to only the risks the architects already know how to solve, and lets the full, sometimes uncomfortable, list of risks reach the stakeholders who need to weigh in on priorities.

The counterpart to a risk is a non-risk: a decision the review team examined and concluded was sound, with a rationale worth recording precisely because someone will eventually ask why it was made that way. A blockchain relying on a well established, widely used price oracle network that aggregates many independent data sources rather than one exchange is a candidate non-risk for the same manipulation scenario, provided the review team can point to the aggregation and the number of independent sources as the reason the risk does not apply.

Individual risks, identified one scenario at a time, can look like isolated engineering issues. The next chapter shows what happens when a review team steps back and notices that many of the individual risks it found actually share a common root cause.
